title: Mysterious move has true believers buzzing: 'Why is all this Bigfoot stuff happening now?'

content:
The U.S. Forest Service has broken its long silence on Bigfoot, and enthusiasts are wondering whether the government is finally ready to spill its secrets.

The Washington Post reported the agency, without any announcement, posted three historical documents on Oct. 15 to its online Freedom of Information Act reading room under the heading “Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records,” which describe reported encounters in Montana and Washington state, some dating back to 1941.

“Why is all this cryptid and Bigfoot-related stuff happening now?” asked Jeremiah Byron, host of the “Bigfoot Society” podcast.

The release came as the Trump administration has been unsealing government files on UFOs, which the Pentagon now calls “Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena.” One of those Defense Department releases, a 2010 report on a Utah ranch, included witness accounts of “dog-like creatures” more than 6 feet tall walking upright, but hair samples collected there turned out to come from dogs and a raccoon.

“I’m hoping what this means is that they could be ramping up government entities to start releasing information about Bigfoot,” Byron told the Post. “People need to be aware it’s the right time to come forward and talk about what you’ve seen, if the government’s starting to talk about it.”

A Forest Service spokesman offered little explanation, telling the Post only that the USDA posts records online when it expects strong public interest when deciding what to post online.

But the agency’s own employees have been less reserved. At an Oct. 8 forum called “Bigfoot in Your Backyard,” held at California’s Stanislaus National Forest near Yosemite, staffer Kathy Marquez described the creature to a packed room.

“He smells bad, he screams, he howls, wood knocks and whistles,” Marquez said. “All sizes from little to big, male and female, have been seen.”

Kathy Strain, the forest’s archaeologist, told attendees there have been 65 recorded sightings in her stretch of the Sierra Nevada, and she claims to have seen two of the creatures herself in Oklahoma’s Ouachita Mountains in 2012, an experience that left her with a “mild panic attack.”

One of the newly posted files covers a 1982 investigation in Washington’s Umatilla National Forest, here part-time patrolman Paul Freeman reported a sighting and later found tracks. A wildlife biologist and a Border Patrol tracker concluded the prints were fake, but the late anthropologist Grover Krantz insisted they were real.

Freeman’s son, Michael, welcomed the release.

“Any and all information should be released,” he said. “Nobody is trying to hide anything.”

The scientific consensus remains firmly skeptical, since no body, droppings or convincing footage has ever turned up, and a new documentary, “Capturing Bigfoot,” recently concluded that the famous 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film was a hoax.

Even the Forest Service hedged its bets. The Stanislaus forum closed with a disclaimer that the forest “cannot confirm or deny the existence of Bigfoot.”
